primary_sources.title: Ghana: The Autobiography of Kwame Nkrumah

secondary_sources.title: Kwame Nkrumah: The Father of African Nationalism

contested_points: Published birth dates vary between 1909 and 1912; colonial school records and later accounts do not fully agree.
Historians debate how far economic planning alone drove early post-independence setbacks versus external shocks and governance choices.
known_myths: No single leader personally delivered independence without parties, unions, and mass movements.
Popular retellings sometimes treat Pan-African congresses as instant political unity rather than contested, gradual coalitions.

retrieval_cards.text: Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957 with Nkrumah as Prime Minister; the Convention People's Party had campaigned on self-government and anti-colonial unity.
Nkrumah promoted Pan-African congresses and wrote that African unity was necessary to resist neo-colonial economic control; outcomes remained politically uneven across states.
Scholarship traces his education in the Gold Coast, the United States, and Britain, including Lincoln University and later political organizing among African students and workers.
A military coup removed Nkrumah from office in February 1966 while he was abroad; he lived in exile afterward and died in 1972.
Nkrumah describes Nzema heritage and childhood in the Gold Coast; language-learning quests may introduce Nzema phrases only from approved teaching notes, not invented forms.
